\chapter*{The Kannada script --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Kannada script (reference)}
\markboth{Kannada script}{Kannada script}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — a place to look things up. You are \emph{not} meant to read this before the lessons: the lessons teach reading through real words, introducing each letter as a word needs it. This page just gathers the system in one spot.

\section*{How the Kannada script works (the three facts the lessons teach)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \kn{ಕ} = \textquotedblleft{}ka,\textquotedblright{} \kn{ಮ} = \textquotedblleft{}ma,\textquotedblright{} \kn{ರ} = \textquotedblleft{}ra.\textquotedblright{} You never write the short \emph{a} — it's already there.
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign changes that built-in vowel.} Attached to a consonant it gives \kn{ಕಾ} = kā · \kn{ಕಿ} = ki · \kn{ಕೀ} = kī · \kn{ಕು} = ku · \kn{ಕೂ} = kū · \kn{ಕೆ} = ke · \kn{ಕೇ} = kē · \kn{ಕೊ} = ko · \kn{ಕೋ} = kō · \kn{ಕೌ} = kau. The signs themselves are \textbf{\kn{ಾ}} ā · \textbf{\kn{ಿ}} i · \textbf{\kn{ೀ}} ī · \textbf{\kn{ು}} u · \textbf{\kn{ೂ}} ū · \textbf{\kn{ೆ}} e · \textbf{\kn{ೇ}} ē · \textbf{\kn{ೊ}} o · \textbf{\kn{ೋ}} ō · \textbf{\kn{ೌ}} au.
  \item \textbf{A \emph{virama} (\kn{್}) strips the built-in vowel, and the bare consonant \emph{stacks under} the next as a conjunct (\emph{ottakṣara}).} \kn{ಸ್} + \kn{ಕ} $\to$ \kn{ಸ್ಕ} (ska), \kn{ನ್} + \kn{ಯ} $\to$ \kn{ನ್ಯ} (nya), \kn{ಲ್} + \kn{ಲ} $\to$ \kn{ಲ್ಲ} (lla). This vertical stacking is a signature of the Kannada–Telugu scripts.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Independent vowels (word-initial)}

When a word \emph{starts} with a vowel, a full vowel letter is used: \textbf{\kn{ಅ}} a · \textbf{\kn{ಆ}} ā · \textbf{\kn{ಇ}} i · \textbf{\kn{ಈ}} ī · \textbf{\kn{ಉ}} u · \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} ū · \textbf{\kn{ಎ}} e · \textbf{\kn{ಏ}} ē · \textbf{\kn{ಐ}} ai · \textbf{\kn{ಒ}} o · \textbf{\kn{ಓ}} ō · \textbf{\kn{ಔ}} au.

\section*{Worth flagging}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Aspiration is written.} \kn{ಕ} k / \kn{ಖ} kh, \kn{ಗ} g / \kn{ಘ} gh, \kn{ದ} d / \kn{ಧ} dh — the \textquotedblleft{}h\textquotedblright{} is a real puff. Unlike Tamil, Kannada keeps separate letters for the Sanskrit aspirates and voiced stops, because it borrowed so many Sanskrit words.
  \item \textbf{Round forms.} Kannada's looping letters were shaped for palm-leaf writing, where straight strokes would split the leaf. Telugu, its closest script-sister, shares the look — which is why the two scripts resemble each other far more than either resembles Tamil.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Kannada in the Dravidian family}

Kannada is one of the four literary \textbf{Dravidian} languages, with Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam — a family entirely separate from the Indo-European one (English, Latin, Sanskrit). It shares grammar and much native vocabulary with its sisters — but, like Telugu and unlike Tamil, it borrowed \textbf{heavily} from Sanskrit. The lessons trace, word by word, which Kannada words are home-grown (\emph{haudu}, \emph{illa}, \emph{sari}) and which came from Sanskrit (\emph{namaskāra}, \emph{dhanyavāda}).
